title: Runbook Automation
description: Convert manual incident response steps into automated runbooks using Linux shell scripts, systemd, and Git-backed documentation.

data.text: A runbook is step-by-step documentation for a specific operational task. When runbooks are automated, they become reproducible, testable, and safe to run at 3 AM when the primary responder is half asleep.
This lesson teaches you how to write, version, and automate runbooks using Git and Linux shell scripting, turning tribal knowledge into institutional memory.

Good runbooks are specific, tested, and versioned. They include the exact commands, expected outputs, and rollback steps. If a teammate cannot follow the runbook without asking questions, it needs improvement.

items: One goal per runbook: restart service, rotate logs, failover database
Show exact commands with expected output
Add rollback steps for every action
Note the last tested date and who tested it

data.title: Sample runbook: restart payment-api
data.code:
Title: Restart Payment API
Service: payment-api
Owner: Platform Team
Last Tested: 2026-09-20

Prerequisites:
- SSH access to app-server-01
- deploy group sudo privileges

Steps:
1. SSH into app-server-01
2. Check service status: sudo systemctl status payment-api
3. Restart service: sudo systemctl restart payment-api
4. Verify health: curl -f http://localhost:3000/health
5. Check logs: sudo journalctl -u payment-api --since '1 min ago'

Rollback:
- sudo systemctl stop payment-api
- sudo systemctl start previous-version.service

data.text: Not every runbook needs a full script, but common high-stakes tasks deserve automation. A scripted runbook runs the same way every time, logs its actions, and returns a clear exit code.

data.title: Automated disk cleanup runbook
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

THRESHOLD=90
EMAIL="ops@example.com"

check_disk() {
  usage=$(df /var/log | awk 'NR==2 {print $5}' | tr -d '%')
  echo "Disk usage: ${usage}%"
  if [ "$usage" -gt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
    echo "WARNING: Disk usage above ${THRESHOLD}%"
    sudo find /var/log -type f -name '*.gz' -mtime +7 -delete
    echo "Old logs cleaned"
  fi
}

log_action() {
  echo "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) - $1" >> /var/log/runbook.log
}

log_action "Disk cleanup started"
check_disk
log_action "Disk cleanup completed"

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: Automated runbooks can cause damage if they contain incorrect logic. Always test runbooks in a staging environment, require peer review for changes, and log every action for auditability.
Store runbooks in a Git repository alongside application code. Use Markdown for readability and pull requests for changes. This gives you history, review, and discoverability in one place.

items: Keep runbooks in a dedicated runbooks/ directory
Require pull request reviews for all changes
Tag runbook versions with application releases
Link runbooks from alert annotations in Alertmanager
Write one runbook for every SEV1 and SEV2 scenario
Test each runbook in staging monthly
Store runbooks in Git with review requirements
Automate repetitive runbooks with shell scripts
Link runbooks from alerts so responders find them instantly

data.title: Summary
data.text: Runbook automation transforms tribal knowledge into reliable, repeatable operations. Write clear steps, automate common tasks, version everything in Git, and test runbooks regularly. When incidents happen at 3 AM, a good runbook is the best teammate you have.
